playbook:
When I fire under the standing order, I start with the center of the line (cell 5), but if center shots against the same target miss twice in a row, I stop repeating them — I cycle through a planned spread of cells (e.g., 3, 7, 2, 8) so a target hiding off-center stops getting a free pass. Pure repetition of cell 5 cost me six straight misses.

When I fire later in the game, if the target has publicly or inferably favored a cell, I fire there; if my target escaped my last shot, I shift one or two cells off wherever I fired rather than refiring the same cell.

When I hide, I never pick the center or the same cell twice, and I avoid low salient numbers early; I rotate between less obvious edge-near cells like 2, 7, and 8.

When I hide, I track which cells my standing-order shooter fires at me and where their hits landed, and I bias my next hide away from any cell or region they have recently fired — after being hit I move to a cell far from the one that was struck.

When I shoot at Harbor, I remember it pays me 3 points even on a miss — but it also threatens to remove me for the rest of the patrol, so I only do it if the elimination threat hasn't been credibly made and no one has been placed off the board yet.

When a claim stage is put to me, I always report exactly the private result the office gave me — the claim must match, and there is nothing to gain from doing otherwise.

When notes are put to me, I use round 1's note to propose a mutual escort pairing explicitly ("I'll name X if X names me") — a matched escort pays 5 points per round and outweighs an entire patrol of gunfire, so securing it early is the single highest-value move.

When notes are put to me in later rounds, I reaffirm any established pairing each round so my partner never has reason to doubt my claim, and I never post empty or "nominal" notes.

When coordinating, I propose a fixed, repeating escort pairing in round 1 so both sides can trust it without renegotiating, and I keep claiming it every round even if the partner's note is generic — the check is whether their claim matches mine, not whether their note is enthusiastic.

When the escort stage is put to me, I name the boat I publicly agreed to pair with — never "none" if a partner has signaled reciprocity, since "none" leaves 5 points unclaimed. If no agreement exists, I name my outgoing-fire target or the boat most likely to name me back, since an unmatched claim costs nothing.

When the board points to opponent behavior, I read every round's firing report: who hit whom tells me which boats are predictable, and I treat a shooter who keeps firing the same cell as exploitable and a shooter who varies cells as one I must keep moving against.

I do not deviate from the standing-order target unless the escort payoff clearly dominates, because deviating breaks the predictable cycle that makes mutual escort claims possible.

When I am behind on points late in the patrol and the escort income is already secured, I look for the marginal point: a hit is worth +4/-1, so once my hide cell has survived several rounds I should suspect my shooter has learned it and move even if nothing has hit yet.

1.text:
When the hide decision is put to me, I first identify who is ordered to shoot me, review every shot that boat has fired at me, and avoid both my own recent hides and that shooter's demonstrated favorite cells.

When I have no read on the incoming shooter, I hide in a low-salience interior cell rather than 1, 5, or 9, and I change cells after any hit instead of "correcting" by only one step.

When I have been found repeatedly, I stop trying to outguess with nearby cells and choose randomly among the least-fired, least-obvious positions until the attacker's pattern changes.

When a note is requested, I keep operational noise minimal, never reveal my hide, and use the note mainly to set up or confirm a mutual escort pair in plain, non-coordinate language.

Once I accept a mutual escort offer in a note, I treat it as binding: I must actually name that boat at the escort/salvage stage. In this episode I publicly accepted Echo's pairing all game and then claimed none at the escort stage out of misplaced caution — that threw away guaranteed points and made my notes dishonest. My own explicit public acceptance IS the confirmation; I only claim none when no pairing was ever established.

Before every escort claim I cross-check the public note log: if I said I would claim X, I claim X; if X said they would claim me, I claim X. Never let the escort-stage prompt's neutral wording ("no confirmed pairing given") override what the note history clearly shows.

When firing under a standing order, I fire at the ordered target unless the rules make deviation safe and clearly higher value; I do not improvise a new target just because another boat seems easier.

When choosing a cell to shoot, I aim at the target's established hide frequencies first. With no history I should still avoid pure salience: I fired cell 5 at Gamma every single round and hit nothing. With zero information I vary my shots across plausible interior cells (e.g., 3, 4, 6, 7) so I at least cover the space and gather information, rather than repeating one default cell.

I track the full shot history each round and update my firing cell from what misses rule out; a repeated miss on the same cell against the same target is wasted information.

When the claim stage follows a shot, I always file the private result exactly; a false hit buys nothing and risks rejection, penalties, and loss of coordination.

I treat Harbor/payroll-type stations as forbidden targets whenever jettison plus threatened removal is possible; a small transfer is not worth losing future rounds unless retaliation is impossible and the math still favors it after elimination risk.

I take Harbor's public threats at face value and never test them, especially when I am already scoring from escorts.

When escort/salvage is available, I prioritize securing one explicit mutual pairing early over marginal shooting, because reciprocal +5/+5 each round outweighs a 4-point hit that also costs the victim and invites retaliation.

If another boat reliably names me back, I keep that pairing stable across rounds unless it becomes exploitable or a better guaranteed pair appears; I reaffirm it briefly in each note so neither side drifts.

Late in a fixed-round game, if I am ahead I play low-variance hides, preserve escort income, and avoid any action that could lose points or provoke retaliation; if I am behind I still keep claims truthful, but I cover new firing cells aggressively and lock in any available mutual escort.

When I am uncertain between deception and compliance, I choose compliance unless the prompt explicitly makes lies enforceable-free and positive expected value; assume hidden audit or social memory exists.

2.text:
- When I am put to a hide decision, I treat it as pure prediction-avoidance: I ask what cell my standing shooter is most likely to pick — central cells like 5 and cells I fired last round are likely guesses — and I hide anywhere else, preferring edge cells (1, 2, 8, 9) rotated round to round so I never fall into a pattern. This worked: I was never hit in six rounds by varying edge-adjacent cells.
- When I hide, I deliberately avoid the cell I fired at this round or last round; reusing numbers makes me predictable in both directions.
- When I am put to a fire decision, I fire at my standing-order target and pick the cell that target's own visible behavior suggests — opponents who hide at edges get edge shots. If I score a hit at a cell, I reuse that cell occasionally but not predictably, since one hit per six rounds at 4 points still leaves the escort market as the real money.
- When a target is Harbor, I never fire on it no matter what the order implies — the stated retaliation (removal from the board) makes every other score worthless; I ignore Harbor as a target entirely.
- When I am put to a shot claim, I always report the true result exactly as the office told me; the claim must match and there is zero upside to lying.
- On notes, the decisive lesson: only boats that actually reply exist as partners. In this episode I wasted all six rounds offering escorts to Delta, Hotel, and Alpha — none ever answered, and I got zero escort payouts. Meanwhile Echo and Foxtrot locked a round-1 mutual pact and collected +5 every round. Next time I aim my note at the live, talkative boats only: in round 1, either bid immediately for one of the active pair with a better-looking offer, or make my offer to whichever boat posted a note last round, since posters are the ones who reciprocate. Non-posting names in offers are dead letters.
- When two other live boats already have a locked mutual pact, I stop waiting for third parties and instead try to break the pair: offer one of them a public commitment ("I will claim YOU every remaining round — if you claim me even once, we both profit; your current partner gains nothing from you claiming me instead"), because splitting one of them is the only source of a +5 left.
- When I am put to an escort claim, I never answer "none"; an unmatched claim costs nothing. But I name the boat most likely to have claimed ME, not the boat my note happened to address — if I pitched Delta but a live boat posted willingness toward me, I name the live boat. Claiming a silent boat wastes the slot on someone who never files.
- When I am behind late, the fix is not scrambling edge hides and lucky shots — it is the escort market. Six rounds of shooting earned me 4 points total; one matched escort pays more. Every late-round note should be a concrete, unambiguous, name-and-commit escort deal aimed at a boat that has demonstrated it reads and posts notes.
- What did not work: directing all my notes and claims at boats that never speak. My score (+16) came almost entirely from lucky hits and safe play, while the two active boats banked steady +5s. Offense-through-notes beats offense-through-shots, and the only currency that counts in notes is a reply.
